unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4! This unit is all about inventions and creativity — two powerful forces that have shaped the world we live in today. Throughout history, people have looked at problems around them and imagined new ways to solve them. From the simple wheel to the complex machines of the modern age, every invention began as an idea in somebody’s mind. In this unit, you will explore how inventions work, why they matter, and how ordinary people — including young people just like you — have changed the world with creative thinking.
unit.learningPath: Preview the unit goals and the six vocabulary groups. Read the information text 'Inventions That Changed Everyday Life' and the three parts of the story 'The Last Straits', then answer the comprehension questions with evidence from the text. Work through the six grammar sections on the past simple, will and won't, prepositional verbs and sequencing words. Complete the six activities, record the speaking tasks, and draft the invention description and a fair-share proposal. Finish with the checkpoint quiz and the self-assessment.

readings.title: Inventions That Changed Everyday Life
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
For thousands of years, human beings have solved problems by inventing new tools and machines. Some inventions were simple, like the wheel or the needle, but they changed life forever. Others were complex, like the printing press or the electric generator, and they opened doors that nobody had imagined before.
One of the most important inventions in history was the compass. Before the compass existed, sailors relied on the stars for navigation. If clouds covered the sky, ships lost their way. Chinese inventors created the first magnetic compass over a thousand years ago. Once sailors had this tool, they explored new territories, crossed dangerous straits, and connected civilizations that had never met before. The compass did not just change travel; it changed the way humans understood the whole world.
Another invention that transformed daily life was the printing press. In the year 1440, a German inventor named Johannes Gutenberg proposed a machine that could print books quickly. Before his invention, every book was copied by hand, which took months. The printing press made books cheaper and easier to produce. Within a few decades, millions of people who had never owned a book could finally read and learn. Knowledge was no longer something only the elite controlled; it belonged to everyone.
In the modern era, the electric generator changed how people lived and worked. A generator converts movement into electricity. Once communities had electricity, they could light their homes, power machines, and store food safely. In many parts of East Africa and the wider world, generators still provide power to schools, hospitals, and homes that are not connected to the main electricity grid. A single generator can make the difference between a community that struggles in the dark and one that thrives with light.
Today, young inventors continue to solve real problems. In Kenya, a teenager invented a device that keeps lions away from livestock by using flashing lights. In Somalia, students have built simple solar-powered chargers so that families in rural areas can charge their phones. These inventions show that you do not need a big laboratory or a lot of money to make a difference; you need curiosity, creativity, and commitment.
Every great invention started with a question: What if? What if we could fly? What if we could talk to someone on the other side of the world? What if we could make clean water from the sea? The inventors who changed history did not have all the answers. They had the courage to ask questions, try new ideas, and learn from their mistakes. That is the true procedure of invention: observe, question, experiment, and improve. And it is a procedure that anyone, including you, can follow.

readings.title: A Gadget You Could Build: The SunJar
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Some of the best inventions are simple enough for a young person to build. Across the world, students are proving that you do not need an expensive laboratory to make a difference. You need a real problem, a clear idea, and the commitment to keep trying.
Think about the SunJar, a gadget a learner could design today. Many children in rural areas cannot study in the evening because their homes do not have electricity. Without light, students quickly fall behind in their schoolwork, so this is a serious problem worth solving.
The SunJar is a glass jar with a small solar panel fixed to the lid and a tiny battery stored inside. During the day, the user places the jar in direct sunlight. The solar panel collects energy and stores it in the battery. First, you open the lid and check the battery level. Next, you set the jar on a table or hang it from a hook. Then you press the button on the side. Finally, the jar fills with bright, warm light that can last for several hours.
If families and schools use inventions like the SunJar, children will be able to study after sunset, and they will not need expensive fuel or candles. A creative idea, built from everyday materials, can change how a whole community lives and learns.

readings.title: The Last Straits, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Long ago, before satellites mapped every coastline, explorers relied on wind, stars, and memory. In the heart of East Africa, a young physicist named Tariq joined a desert caravan setting out toward the unknown.
Their goal was to cross the Mzingi Straits, a mysterious water passage between two towering cliffs. No one had returned alive, but old maps claimed an extended river system ran beneath the cliffs. If it were true, the discovery could help small communities relocate and survive years of drought.
Tariq's team consisted of eight people: two experienced explorers, a weather expert in meteorology, a translator, and a group of local guides who knew the sands well. Each of them had made a serious commitment to the mission, not for glory, but to bring change.
The team's leader, Amara, stood before a map made of stitched cloth. Her hands, rough from years of expeditions, smoothed the fabric as if it held secrets.
'We will travel through harsh terrain,' she said. 'But if we succeed, this discovery will change how people understand the region.'
Tariq asked, 'What will we do if the riverbed is dry?'
'We will adapt,' Amara replied. 'The initiative depends on our resolve.'
Their first camp was near a cluster of acacia trees. Tariq set up a generator to power their tools. The machine hummed across the sand, pulsing like a second heart for the team.
'This generator is our lifeline,' he told the group. 'Without it, we cannot track the weather or charge our equipment.'
Each morning, they rose early to record data. Tariq explained the procedure to the younger guides.
'First, we collect samples. Then we label and store them carefully. Finally, we submit our findings to the agency.'
The young guides nodded. 'You are not like other outsiders,' one of them said. 'You explain things.'
Tariq smiled. 'Good science starts by listening.'
By the third week, the desert turned treacherous. Sandstorms appeared without warning. One storm destroyed their water cart.
'We must extend the trip,' Amara said. 'We will stop in the next territory for supplies.'
They relied on nearby nomads, who shared dried meat and sour milk in exchange for medicine and solar batteries.
'These people follow the herds and the stars,' Amara explained. 'They have navigated these sands for generations.'
At night, Tariq taught a young boy how to use the compass and read the clouds. In return, the boy sang desert songs that described the stars like friends.
One evening, just after dusk, a lone man arrived on camelback. His cloak was sun-bleached and torn, but his manner was sharp and calm.
'I am Karim,' he said. 'I have lived near the straits. I have seen what lies beyond.'
'An eyewitness account?' Amara asked. 'Can you describe it?'

readings.title: The Last Straits, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
'I saw water rushing like thunder,' Karim said. 'But I also saw markers, skulls set on posts. Someone refused to let strangers pass.'
'Who controls it now?' Tariq asked.
Karim shrugged. 'A forgotten civilization, or a violent faction. Maybe both.'
Tariq looked again at the fading map. 'We will proceed carefully. We are not here to fight.'
The caravan reached the cliffs two days later. The wind screamed through the narrow passages. Rock carvings lined the stone, figures with long limbs and shields.
'This is a warning,' Karim said. 'But it is also confirmation.'
Using climbing gear, the team descended. At the base, they found smooth black stones, and in the cracks, cool mist was rising.
'There is water,' Tariq whispered. 'We were right.'
Then they saw dozens of footprints and a camp that had been abandoned recently. The fires were still warm. Tools lay half-buried in the dust.
'They must have relocated in a hurry,' Amara said. 'But why?'
Among the ashes, they found scraps of paper covered in code. One word had not burned: segregation.
Amara frowned. 'This is no longer just a river expedition. Someone tried to control who passed, and who drank.'
'Because if you control the land, you control the people,' Tariq said. 'And if you control the water, you control life.'
They set up a base higher on the ridge. Tariq reconnected the generator and began measuring the water speed, purity, and flow.
'We must regulate how this water is used,' he said. 'It cannot belong to any one group.'
Amara added, 'We are not just explorers. We are stewards of what we find.'
That night, the team wrote a proposal to explain what the land offered, and why it had to remain open.
'We propose an open science zone,' they wrote. 'This land should not be claimed by any one nation. Its production of clean water must support all the nearby communities. We must resist any system that repeats the segregation of the past.'
They added their predictions. If the area were claimed by force, violence would follow. If it were shared peacefully, migration and farming would improve.
'Real exploration begins with respect,' Tariq wrote. 'We do not own this place. We study, we learn, and we serve.'
As the team packed to leave, one member uncovered a rusted metal plate buried in the sand, its letters barely readable.
Karim pointed at it. 'A failed empire,' he said. 'They built walls, and they were erased.'
The journey home was long. Tariq taught the young guides to track the clouds and draw their own maps. In return, the boys sang to him, songs that had guided travellers for centuries.
Back in the capital, Amara delivered the report to the agency.
'The initiative is complete,' she said. 'But the river is still flowing.'
A year later, schools across East Africa studied the Mzingi discovery. Wells were dug. No flag flew over the cliffs, and the water remained free.

readings.title: The Last Straits, part 3
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Years later, Tariq gave talks at universities about the expedition. 'What does science consist of?' he would ask. 'It consists of questions, care, and courage.'
He always ended with a photograph of Amara, Karim, the young guides, and himself, standing together by the straits with notebooks in hand and red cloths tied to signal peace.
'Explorers may map the land,' he would say. 'But true exploration maps the future.'
And deep beneath the cliffs, the river still ran, untouched and unowned, waiting for the next ones who would come, not to take, but to understand.

comprehension.question: What problem does the SunJar solve, and how does it work?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It gives light to children whose homes have no electricity by storing sunlight in a battery inside a glass jar.
comprehension.explanation: Reading 2 explains that the SunJar collects solar energy during the day and releases it as light so learners can study after sunset.

comprehension.question: According to Reading 2, what does a young inventor really need in order to make a difference?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A real problem to solve, a clear idea, and the commitment to keep trying, rather than an expensive laboratory.
comprehension.explanation: Reading 2 states that a young inventor needs a real problem, a clear idea and commitment instead of an expensive laboratory or a lot of money.

comprehension.question: Who is Tariq, and what is his role in the expedition?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Tariq is a young physicist who joined the caravan and ran the generator and the data collection for the team.
comprehension.explanation: Part 1 introduces Tariq as a young physicist who set up the generator and taught the guides the procedure for collecting data.

comprehension.question: Why did Tariq call the generator the team's 'lifeline'?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Because without it the team could not track the weather or charge their equipment out in the desert.
comprehension.explanation: In Part 1 Tariq says that without the generator they cannot track the weather or charge their equipment, which is why it is their lifeline.

comprehension.question: What single word did the team find among the ashes, and what did it reveal?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They found the word 'segregation', which revealed that someone had tried to control who could pass and who could drink.
comprehension.explanation: In Part 2 the one unburned word, segregation, shows that a group had tried to keep others away from the water.

comprehension.question: What did the team propose about the water, and why?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They proposed an open science zone so the clean water could not be claimed by one nation and would support every nearby community.
comprehension.explanation: Part 2 records the team's written proposal for an open science zone that keeps the water free for all nearby communities.

comprehension.question: Amara says the team are 'stewards of what we find.' What does being a steward mean here?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A steward looks after something for everyone instead of owning it, so the team protect the water rather than claim it.
comprehension.explanation: Part 2 shows the team acting as stewards by regulating the water and keeping it open to all rather than taking it for themselves.

grammar.title: Past Simple Tense (Reviewed)
grammar.explanation: The past simple tense describes actions that happened at a definite time in the past and are now finished, which is why we use it when we talk about inventions and discoveries.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Regular verbs add -ed to the base form, so play becomes played and claim becomes claimed. When a verb ends in a silent e, add only -d, so propose becomes proposed. After a short vowel, double the final consonant, so travel becomes travelled. Change a final y to i after a consonant, so carry becomes carried. Irregular verbs must be memorised: go became went, see became saw, make became made, write became wrote, have became had, find became found, and build became built.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often forget to change the verb at all, writing 'I play football yesterday' when a finished past action needs 'I played football yesterday'.
grammar.memoryTip: Picture the past simple as a time machine: regular verbs travel back on an -ed ticket, while each irregular verb needs its own special ticket learned by heart.
grammar.practice:
Part A: rewrite eight base verbs (claim, propose, visit, relocate, regulate, refuse, monitor, travel) in the past simple. Part B: complete eight sentences about the expedition using the irregular pasts of make, go, write, find, have, see, build and run.

ANSWER KEY (self-check — complete Parts A and B first, then check your work): Part A: claim -> claimed, propose -> proposed, visit -> visited, relocate -> relocated, regulate -> regulated, refuse -> refused, monitor -> monitored, travel -> travelled (double the final consonant after a short vowel). Part B: make -> made, go -> went, write -> wrote, find -> found, have -> had, see -> saw, build -> built, run -> ran.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Will and Won't for Predictions
grammar.explanation: We use will and won't to predict what we think the future holds, which helps us share ideas about how new inventions might change our lives.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: For a positive prediction, use subject plus will plus the base verb, as in 'The invention will help many people.' For a negative prediction, use subject plus won't plus the base verb, as in 'They won't finish if they waste time.' Add I think, I believe or I am sure to show how certain you are, so 'I am sure the project will succeed' sounds more confident than 'I think it will rain tomorrow'.
grammar.commonMistake: A common error is adding -s to the verb after will, as in 'She will eats the cake'; after will or won't the verb always stays in its base form, so it must be 'She will eat the cake'.
grammar.memoryTip: Treat will as a firm yes to the future and won't as a clear no, then ask yourself whether your prediction is a yes or a no before you write it.
grammar.practice:
Complete six predictions about future inventions using will or won't, then justify two of your predictions with a reason introduced by because.

ANSWER KEY (self-check — this task is open-ended, so there is no single fixed answer): Compare your six predictions and two justifications to this model, grounded in the unit's own inventions theme: 'Solar-powered gadgets will replace battery-powered ones because they will not run out of power outdoors.' 'Simple household robots won't disappear because families will still want help with daily chores.' 'New medical scanners will detect illness earlier.' Check each prediction: does it use will or won't plus the base verb, with no -s added (will help, not will helps)? For your two justified predictions, does each because clause give a real reason, the way Amara does in the story: 'We will adapt... The initiative depends on our resolve'?
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Prepositional Verbs
grammar.explanation: A prepositional verb is a verb joined to a fixed preposition that gives it a precise meaning, so choosing the right preposition keeps the sentence correct.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Some verbs always travel with one particular preposition: rely on, travel through, wait for, set out from and consist of. We say 'I rely on my friends', 'we travel through the desert', 'please wait for me', 'they set out from the camp at dawn' and 'the team consists of eight members'.
grammar.commonMistake: Writers sometimes drop the preposition, turning 'I rely on my friends' into the incomplete 'I rely my friends', or swap it for the wrong one, as in 'I travel over the city' instead of 'I travel through the city'.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of each verb and its preposition as best friends who always stay together; separate them and the meaning changes or disappears.
grammar.practice:
Choose the correct preposition to finish six sentences (rely on, travel through, wait for, set out from, consist of), then write two sentences of your own that each use a different prepositional verb.

ANSWER KEY (self-check — complete the six gap-fill sentences first, then check your work): whatever the exact wording of your six sentences, each of these prepositional verbs only ever takes one partner: rely on, travel through, wait for, set out from, consist of (one pair is used twice across the six sentences). Example from the story: 'explorers relied on wind, stars, and memory' and "Tariq's team consisted of eight people." The second part (write two of your own sentences) is open-ended — there is no single correct answer. Self-check instead: did you choose two different prepositional verbs from the list, and does each one keep its fixed preposition, as in 'We waited for the guide' or 'They set out from the camp at dawn'?
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Past Simple: Negatives and Questions
grammar.explanation: To say what did not happen, or to ask about the past, we combine did with the base form of the main verb rather than a second past-tense verb.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Make a negative with did not, or the short form didn't, plus the base verb: 'She did not see the machine.' Make a question with Did plus the subject plus the base verb: 'Did the physicist propose a theory?' The short answers are 'Yes, she did' and 'No, she didn't'. The main verb never changes to its past form once did is in the sentence.
grammar.commonMistake: The past form often slips back in after did, giving 'She did not went' or 'Did you went?'; because did already carries the past meaning, the base verb is needed, as in 'She did not go' and 'Did you go?'.
grammar.memoryTip: Remember that did is the only word that time-travels; once did has done the job, every verb behind it stays in its plain base form.
grammar.practice:
Part A: rewrite five statements as negatives using did not. Part B: turn four statements into past simple questions beginning with Did, then reply to each with a short answer.

ANSWER KEY (self-check — the exact statements are on your worksheet, so use this pattern check rather than a fixed list): Part A: every negative must use did not/didn't plus the base verb, never the past-tense form, as in 'She did not see the machine' (not 'she did not saw') and 'Tariq did not build the generator alone.' Part B: every question must begin with Did plus the subject plus the base verb, and every short answer must repeat did/didn't rather than the full verb, as in 'Did the physicist propose a theory? Yes, he did.' and 'Did the team find water? Yes, they did.' Check each of your own answers against this pattern.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Sequencing Words for Presenting
grammar.explanation: Sequencing words signal the order of steps, so a listener or reader can follow an explanation of how an invention or a procedure works.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Use First for the opening step, Next or Then for the steps that follow, After that for a later step, and Finally for the last one. For example: 'First, we explored the straits. Then we set up a research site. After that, we collected samples from the water. Finally, we wrote our report.'
grammar.commonMistake: Presenters often join every step with and, so the order blurs; replacing some of those ands with First, Then and Finally makes the sequence clear.
grammar.memoryTip: Imagine your steps as a numbered ladder: First is the bottom rung and Finally is the top, and the sequencing words are the rungs the listener climbs.
grammar.practice:
Put four jumbled steps of a simple procedure into order using First, Then, After that and Finally, then use the same four words to explain how your own invention works.

ANSWER KEY (self-check — the four jumbled steps are on your worksheet, so check the connecting words rather than the step content): whatever the four steps describe, the sequencing words themselves always go in this order: First, then Then, then After that, then Finally, as in the story's own example: 'First, we collect samples. Then we label and store them carefully. Finally, we submit our findings to the agency.' The second part (explain how your own invention works) is open-ended — there is no single correct answer. Self-check instead: did you use each of the four sequencing words exactly once, in that order, with one clear step after each one?
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Editing and Applying Unit Grammar
grammar.explanation: Strong writers revise a whole paragraph, checking that the past simple, predictions with will, prepositional verbs and sequencing words all work together for meaning and flow.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Read your paragraph aloud and check one feature at a time: are the past simple verbs formed correctly, do will and won't keep the base verb, are the prepositional verbs paired with the right preposition, and do the sequencing words guide the reader? Fix one feature before you move to the next.
grammar.commonMistake: Editors sometimes change words at random without checking that the paragraph still means the same thing; every change should have a clear reason behind it.
grammar.memoryTip: Follow four steps in order: read, notice, revise, then reread to be sure the meaning survived the change.
grammar.practice:
Edit a three-paragraph invention description, mark six improvements to tense, prepositions, predictions and sequencing, then explain in a sentence how three of those changes improved the writing.

ANSWER KEY (self-check — editing your own three paragraphs is open-ended, so there is no single fixed answer): check each of your six marked improvements against the unit's four rules — tense (every finished past action uses past simple, e.g. 'built', not 'builded'), prepositions (each prepositional verb keeps its one fixed partner, such as rely on or consist of), predictions (will/won't is always followed by the base verb, e.g. will help, not will helps), and sequencing (First, Then, After that and Finally appear in that order and guide the reader). For your three written explanations, check that each one names which of these four features you fixed and says specifically how the change made the writing clearer.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

activities.title: Activities 1: Timeline of Inventions
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Create a timeline showing five important inventions. For each one, write the date, the name of the invention, and one sentence about it using the past simple tense.
For example:
Around 3500 BC — The wheel: Early civilizations invented the wheel to carry heavy loads.
Around 1000 AD — The compass: Chinese inventors created the magnetic compass for navigation.
Add at least three more inventions of your choice. You can research them with your AI tutor or use your own knowledge.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 2: Prepositional Verbs Challenge
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Prepositional verbs are verbs that always go with a specific preposition. Complete each sentence with the correct preposition: on, through, for, of, from.
The explorers relied __________ the stars for navigation.
The caravan travelled __________ the desert for three weeks.
We must wait __________ the results of the experiment.
The team consists __________ eight experienced members.
They set out __________ the capital at dawn.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 3: Will and Won’t Predictions
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Make predictions about inventions and the future. Complete each sentence with will or won’t and an idea of your own.
In 50 years, I think cars __________.
I believe schools __________.
I think people __________ use paper books anymore because __________.
Robots __________ do all household tasks because __________.
Clean water __________ be available to everyone if __________.
There are no single right answers for this activity. The important thing is to use will and won’t correctly and give a reason for your prediction.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 4: Vocabulary Crossword Clues
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write a definition or clue for each vocabulary word. Then give your clues to a partner and see if they can guess the word.
A narrow passage of water between two areas of land. (__________)
A person who moves from place to place instead of having one home. (__________)
A machine that produces electricity. (__________)
To say no to something or not accept it. (__________)
The study of weather and how it changes. (__________)
A group of people travelling together, often across a desert. (__________)
To suggest an idea or plan for others to think about. (__________)
A person who sees something happen with their own eyes. (__________)
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 5: Write a Short Report
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Choose one famous inventor or invention and write a short report of eight to ten sentences. Use the past simple tense to describe what happened. Include who the inventor was and where they lived, what problem they wanted to solve, what they invented and how it worked, and how the invention changed people's lives.
Here are some suggestions: the telephone (Alexander Graham Bell), the light bulb (Thomas Edison), the astrolabe (early astronomers), or the printing press (Johannes Gutenberg). You can also choose someone else with the help of your AI tutor.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

A strong report names the inventor and where they lived, the problem, the invention and how it worked, and how it changed lives, all in the past simple, for example a report on Johannes Gutenberg and the printing press.
Accept any clear sorting of twelve unit words into sensible categories, provided the learner states the rule for each category in one complete sentence.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: A narrow body of water between two pieces of land. Straits are a narrow body of water between two pieces of land, as when the ships passed through the straits.
A person who travels to new places to discover things. An explorer travels to new places to discover things, like the explorer who found a new island.
A short trip or journey, usually for fun or learning. An excursion is a short trip or journey, usually for fun or learning, such as a class visit to a museum.
A group of people travelling together, often across a desert. A caravan is a group of people travelling together, often across a desert.
navigation Reading 1 says that before the compass, sailors relied on the stars for navigation.
elite Reading 1 says knowledge was no longer something only the elite controlled.
caravan Reading 3 says Tariq joined a desert caravan setting out toward the unknown.
regulate Reading 4 says the team must regulate how the water is used so it belongs to no single group.
generator Reading 1 explains that a generator converts movement into electricity.
The study of weather and how it changes. Meteorology is the study of weather and how it changes; the expedition included a weather expert in meteorology.
